71.title: Development of the State
71.b0.ask: “Born of war and conquest, how can the state grow into an ideal state that serves liberty, education, and service?”
71.b2.p: In Paper 70 we followed the long evolution of human government, from war to courts and from chiefs to representative rule. Paper 71 examines the institution that stands at the end of that road: the state. The state is a useful evolution of civilization; it represents society's net gain from the ravages and sufferings of war.
71.b3.p: The paper says that the state did not come from a divine source, nor was it wisely designed by anyone. It is purely an evolutionary institution that survived the long struggle for group power, and it was wholly automatic in origin.
71.b4.p: Through what stages, then, did the state born of conquest reach representative government? What does an ideal state do, and what kind of people must its citizens become?
71.b5.q: ⟦Q 71:3.1⟧It is not what a state is but what it does that determines the course of social evolution.⟦/Q⟧
71.b8.p: The state is a territorial social regulative organization, and the strongest and most enduring state is made up of a single nation with a common language, mores, and institutions. The early states were small, all the result of conquest, and therefore stratified from the start. The paper sets the Iroquois federation of the northern red men beside Rome to show what keeps a state alive and what was missing.
71.b9.t: What the Roman state was built on
Acquirement and inheritance of private property
Agriculture and the domestication of animals
Conquest and reorganization of weak peoples
71.b10.p: The red men, the paper says, had a good government but were too democratic; had they not met the white man's civilization too soon, they would eventually have evolved a state. Rome's fall came not from its reforms themselves but from their sudden and extensive adoption, combined with too rapid expansion and internal degeneration. When a state fails to hold together, it slips back to clan and tribal stages, as in the feudalism of the European Middle Ages.
71.b12.p: Democracy is an ideal, but it is a product of civilization, not of evolution. So the paper counsels, “⟦Q 71:2.1⟧Go slowly! select carefully!⟦/Q⟧” and names five dangers. Public opinion delays society, yet it preserves civilization; educating public opinion is the only safe and true way to speed civilization, and cultural growth will accelerate as bullets give way to ballots.
71.b13.t: Failing to recognize the basic facts of social evolution
In the hands of uneducated and indolent majorities
The majority is not always right
71.b14.q: ⟦Q 71:2.8⟧Popular elections may not always decide things rightly, but they represent the right way even to do a wrong thing.⟦/Q⟧
71.b15.p: The paper then sets out ten steps toward practical representative government. They begin with the abolition of every form of bondage and end with electing to office only those who are trained and morally fit. Only in this way can government of the people, by the people, and for the people be preserved.
71.b16.t: Abolishing slavery, serfdom, and all bondage
Without education, freedom does more harm than good
Fundamental law in place of rulers' whims
Freedom of every form of expression
The right to use, sell, and bequeath one's property
The citizen's right to be heard
Petition growing into actual management of government
Electing only the competent and morally fit
71.b18.p: The form of a government matters little so long as it provides liberty, security, education, and social co-ordination. No state can rise above the moral values of its citizens, and ignorance and selfishness will bring down even the highest type of government. The chosen-people doctrine was a prime factor in building nations, yet intolerance is forever hostile to human progress, and it is best fought by the co-ordination of science, commerce, play, and religion.
71.b19.t: Interpreted in terms of planetary facts, needs, and goals
71.b20.p: The ideal state has few laws; it has passed beyond the age of taboo into an era of growing liberty through greater self-control. The leisure that machines provide must produce as well as consume. That state is best which co-ordinates most while governing least, and the level of any civilization is portrayed by the caliber of the citizens who volunteer to bear the responsibilities of statehood. In advanced states, political service is honored as the highest devotion of the citizen.
71.b22.p: Economics, society, and government must evolve if they are to remain; on an evolutionary world, standing still means decay. The paper lists twelve points in the program of an expanding civilization, which lead toward the highest goals of all: the brotherhood of man and God-consciousness.
71.b24.p: Genuine brotherhood means a society in which all delight in bearing one another's burdens and truly wish to practice the golden rule. But idealism cannot survive if idealists allow themselves to be exploited or destroyed, so the “golden rulers” must live by their ideals while keeping an adequate defense. Here lies the great test of idealism. Only religious idealism can keep preparedness from turning into aggression, and only love, brotherhood, can prevent the strong from oppressing the weak.
71.b26.p: Competition is essential to social progress, but unregulated competition breeds violence. Today competition is slowly displacing war. Murder has been outlawed since the early days of society, yet war has never yet been outlawed by mankind as a whole. The ideal state regulates competition only enough to remove violence and unfairness, and it must keep taxation from crippling industry and the state from becoming parasitical or tyrannical.
71.b27.t: Competition — the survival of the biologically fit
Co-operation — intelligent co-operation, understanding fraternity, spiritual brotherhood
71.b28.p: Industrial competition is wasteful and inefficient, but the paper insists that no attempt to remove it should be allowed if it would cost even the slightest loss of the basic liberties of the individual.
71.b30.p: Today's profit-motivated economics is doomed unless profit motives are enlarged by service motives. Ruthless competition based on narrow self-interest destroys even what it seeks to keep, and an exclusive profit motive is incompatible with the teachings of Jesus. Yet the profit motive keeps many otherwise slothful people at work, so it must not be destroyed suddenly. It should remain until people have firmly taken hold of higher, nonprofit motives.
71.b31.t: Superlative wisdom, intriguing brotherhood, excellency of spiritual attainment
71.b33.p: The enduring state is founded on culture, dominated by ideals, and motivated by service. The purpose of education is to acquire skill, pursue wisdom, realize selfhood, and attain spiritual values. In the ideal state education continues throughout life and philosophy becomes the chief pursuit of its citizens. Education must change from localistic, militaristic, and success seeking to world-wide, idealistic, and cosmic grasping; having passed from the clergy to lawyers and businessmen, it must finally be given over to philosophers and scientists.
71.b35.q: ⟦Q 71:7.5⟧Education is the business of living; it must continue throughout a lifetime⟦/Q⟧
71.b36.p: Through these seven levels many will ascend to the mortal ultimate of mind attainment, God-consciousness.
71.b38.p: The only sacred feature of any human government is the division of the state into executive, legislative, and judicial domains, and the universe itself is administered on this plan. Beyond that, it matters little what form of state a people chooses, so long as its citizens keep progressing toward greater self-control and social service. The paper lists twelve levels through which statehood evolves.
71.b39.t: Abolition of every form of slavery
The citizens control the levying of taxes
Learning from the cradle to the grave
Proper adjustment between local and national governments
Co-ordinated functioning of men and women, and women's service
Continental courts and a supreme planetary tribunal
The exaltation of philosophy, heralding light and life
71.b40.p: Urantia is still far from these ideals, but the civilized races have made a beginning, and mankind is on the march toward higher evolutionary destinies.
71.b42.p: Paper 71 calmly shows that the state has no divine origin but arose automatically out of war and conquest. Yet the paper is less interested in where the state came from than in what it does. Representative government must take the long steps of ending bondage, educating minds, and establishing the reign of law and freedom of expression; competition must grow into co-operation, and the profit motive into the service motive. All this becomes possible only when there are citizens who, through education, rise to wisdom and God-consciousness. In the end, a state can rise no higher than the moral values of its citizens.
71.b43.t: The state was born of conquest and held together by territory
Democracy is reached slowly, through ten steps
No state can rise above the moral values of its citizens
Love keeps preparedness from turning into aggression
Competition serves early ages; co-operation serves advanced civilization
The profit motive must slowly grow into the service motive
Lifelong education leads through seven levels of wisdom to God-consciousness
The threefold division of powers is the one sacred feature of government
71.b45.box: A state is judged not by what it is but by what it does, and only educated citizens who serve can raise it into an ideal state.
72.title: Government on a Neighboring Planet
72.b0.ask: “On a neighboring planet that suffered rebellion and default just as we did, how did one nation build an advanced government on the home, education, and service?”
72.b2.p: From Paper 68 through Paper 71 we traced how civilization, institutions, government, and the state evolved on Urantia. Paper 72 turns our eyes outward for a moment. By special permission, a Melchizedek describes the social, moral, and political life of the most advanced human race on a not far-distant planet in the system of Satania.
72.b3.p: Like Urantia, this planet was led astray when its Planetary Prince joined the Lucifer rebellion; its Material Son also defaulted, and it has never received a Magisterial Son, so it remains isolated. Of all the Satania worlds isolated by the rebellion, its history is most like ours, and that is why this unusual account was allowed.
72.b4.p: Under such handicaps, what kind of government, home, education, and industry did one continental nation achieve? And what can we learn from it — and what should we weigh with care?
72.b5.q: ⟦Q 72:11.4⟧They have become civilized to that point where they can vigorously defend civilization⟦/Q⟧
72.b8.p: Despite all the planet's handicaps, a very superior civilization is growing on an isolated continent about the size of Australia. The nation numbers about 140 million, a mixed race, mainly blue and yellow, whose peoples fraternize very acceptably. The average length of life is ninety years. High mountains at the center of the country, with heavy rains, make water power and irrigation easy. The nation is rich in natural resources and wholly self-sustaining, but it has little foreign trade because of the hostility of its neighbors.
72.b9.p: This nation, too, traveled the long road from tribes to kings, then through abortive republics and dictators. About five hundred years ago one of three dictator-triumvirs had a change of heart and offered to step down; the continent was united, and under a strong monarchy a masterful charter of liberty evolved. The change to representative government came gradually, and the present republic has now existed for two hundred years.
72.b11.p: The central government is a strong federation of one hundred comparatively free states. State governors and legislators are elected for ten years and cannot be re-elected, and no city may have more than one million inhabitants. The federal government has three co-ordinate branches — executive, legislative, and judicial. The chief executive is elected every six years by universal suffrage and is advised by a supercabinet made up of all living former chief executives.
72.b12.t: How chosen and what it does
Elected by groups of workers according to economic function — industry, the professions, agriculture
Elected by social, political, and philosophic groups
One hundred veterans of civic service, serving for life — purely advisory
72.b13.p: Much of the federal administration is carried on by ten regional authorities, each made up of ten states. Justice is administered by two court systems. The law courts work on three levels — minor courts, state supreme courts, and the federal supreme court — while the socioeconomic courts work in three divisions.
72.b14.t: The state and regional school systems
The settlement of all economic misunderstandings
72.b16.p: These people regard the home as the basic institution of their civilization. It is against the law for two families to live under one roof; homesites must be generous and are free from taxation. Both fathers and mothers must attend parental schools, and fathers give almost as much attention to child culture as mothers do. To be given the guardianship of an orphan is a great honor, and the orphan goes to the home that shows the best parental qualifications.
72.b17.p: Sex instruction and religious training belong to the home, and religion is seen as an integral part of home life. In their philosophy, religion is the striving to know God and to show love for one's fellows through service; instead of churches, they have only temples of philosophy. Although divorce is easy, the divorce rate is only one tenth that of the civilized races of Urantia.
72.b18.t: The first initiation into civic responsibility
The right to vote; marriage permitted
The right to marry without parental consent
72.b20.p: Education is compulsory from five to eighteen. There are no classrooms, and only one subject is studied at a time. After the first three years every pupil becomes an assistant teacher, instructing those below. Books are used only to help solve problems that arise in the school shops and on the school farms. A quarter of school time goes to competitive athletics, and contests in oratory, music, science, and philosophy run all the way up to national honors.
72.b21.p: The chief aim of education is to make every pupil a self-supporting citizen, so every graduate of eighteen is a skilled artisan; only then does the study of books and special knowledge begin in the adult schools and colleges. The paper records that for seventy-five years this nation has placed the feeble-minded in custodial colonies for life and denied them parenthood.
72.b23.p: Industry in this nation is still far from its ideals, but the workers are increasingly becoming shareholders in every concern, and every intelligent laborer is slowly becoming a small capitalist. When slavery was abolished more than a hundred years ago, it was done gradually, freeing two per cent each year, so no grave economic problems followed. Violence has been outlawed as a way of settling disputes, and all industrial disputes are decided by the industrial courts.
72.b24.t: Legal rates of interest on invested capital
A reasonable salary for the skill employed
72.b25.p: People work four days and play one, six hours a day. Two hundred years ago the profit motive ruled industry, but now competition is moving into play, skill, science, intellectual achievement, and public service. The richest man on the continent works six hours a day and then hurries to the school of statesmanship to qualify for public service. These people have come to feel a disgust for both idleness and unearned wealth, and they are learning the worth of well-earned leisure.
72.b27.p: This nation is working to replace self-respect-destroying charity with dignified insurance for old age. Because it gives every child an education and every man a job, such a plan can succeed. Everyone must retire from gainful work at sixty-five, except government servants and philosophers.
72.b28.t: Collected from everyone, since everyone works
The excess profits of conscript labor
Half the income of this social trust
72.b29.p: These funds have long been honestly administered. Next to treason and murder, the heaviest penalties are attached to betrayal of public trust, and social and political disloyalty are regarded as the most heinous of all crimes.
72.b31.p: The federal government is paternalistic only in old-age pensions and the fostering of genius; the states are a little more so, and local governments much more. Individual and family health remain matters of personal concern only. Cities can neither tax nor go into debt, no property may be taxed more than one per cent of its value in a year, and the federal government itself cannot borrow.
72.b32.t: Protect the continent's high standard of living
Half the profits from inventions and creative works
Graduated from one to fifty per cent
Leased for commercial and recreational use
Income left after its designated purposes
72.b34.p: Besides the basic compulsory education, five kinds of special schools are maintained. The schools of statesmanship are of three classes — national, regional, and state. Public offices fall into four divisions, and the upper three may be held only by graduates of the corresponding schools of statesmanship. Judges of the federal supreme court must hold degrees from all of them.
72.b35.t: Train public officials and judges, in three classes
Affiliated with the temples of philosophy and associated with religion
Technical training for twelve learned professions
Training for volunteers from eighteen to thirty
72.b37.p: Every candidate for public office must be a graduate of a school of statesmanship, yet the nation's leaders saw a serious weakness in universal suffrage and about fifty years ago changed their voting plan. Every man and woman of twenty or over has one vote and belongs to two voting groups: one by economic function, and one by political, philosophic, and social inclination.
72.b38.t: Every citizen of twenty or over, enrolled in two voting groups
Up to nine for those who have shown great service or wisdom
Compulsory laborers in the mines and tax-supported public servants
Five brackets, up to five votes — no one may cast more than ten
By group rather than residence — only the chief executive is chosen one person, one vote
72.b39.p: The paper explains that this nation sees the ideal state as an organism, with every free and intelligent group of citizens a vital organ within it. Believing that the dominance of mediocrity spells the downfall of any nation, they allow proceedings to disenfranchise defective or criminal individuals, and voting is compulsory.
72.b41.p: The paper says at the outset that this people's methods of dealing with crime, insanity, and degeneracy, while in some ways pleasing, will in others prove shocking to most Urantians. Ordinary criminals and defectives live in agricultural colonies separated by sex and are more than self-supporting, and the paper records that serious habitual criminals and the incurably insane are sentenced to death.
72.b42.p: The paper reports that these people are passing from the negative to the positive era of law and are trying to prevent crime. Justice is sure and swift, and the homicide rate is only one per cent of that among other nations. It also explains that for over a hundred years the nation has worked to prevent the breeding of criminals and defectives.
72.b44.p: Graduates of the federal military schools are commissioned as “⟦Q 72:11.1⟧guardians of civilization.⟦/Q⟧” Military training is never given without the mastery of some trade or profession, so that no professional military class arises. Military service in peacetime is voluntary, music is one of the chief subjects of the military schools, and in times of industrial slackness the unemployed are used to build up the nation's defenses.
72.b45.p: The nation keeps a powerful military establishment against its hostile neighbors, yet for over a hundred years it has not used it in an offensive war. Though it has fought nine fierce defensive wars in the last two centuries, it pays far more attention to training statesmen, scientists, and philosophers. In peacetime all its mobile defense equipment is used for trade, commerce, and recreation.
72.b46.q: ⟦Q 72:11.4⟧They have become civilized to that point where they can vigorously defend civilization without yielding to the temptation to utilize their war powers in aggression.⟦/Q⟧
72.b48.p: This planet has eleven continents. This one nation is in many ways superior to the nations of Urantia, but the governments of the other continents are decidedly inferior to Urantia's more advanced nations. The nation now plans to open ambassadorial relations with its neighbors and to send missionaries, and the author fears it may repeat the mistake of so many who tried to force a superior culture on others. How much better, he says, if it brought the best of its neighbors home, educated them, and sent them back as emissaries of culture.
72.b49.t: Neither a magisterial nor a bestowal mission
Very wide between the continental nation and its neighbors
72.b50.p: Because of the bestowal and the Spirit of Truth, the paper says, Urantia is far better prepared for the early realization of a planetary government with its laws, mechanisms, symbols, and language. Such a government could establish world-wide peace under law and lead, through a real age of spiritual striving, to the threshold of light and life.
72.b52.p: Paper 72 shows a planet that suffered the same rebellion and default as ours and never received even a Magisterial Son. There one continental nation made the home the foundation of civilization and built an advanced government on lifelong education, schools of statesmanship, an industry that honors service, and an honestly kept public trust. The paper itself admits that some of that nation's practices would shock Urantians, and it offers the account not as a blueprint to copy but as a comparison to encourage the growth of civilization and government. And in the end it turns to us: Urantia, having received a bestowal Son and the Spirit of Truth, stands on a far better spiritual foundation to prepare for world peace under law and the age of light and life.
72.b53.t: A superior civilization is growing on one continent of an isolated world
A federation of a hundred states, a three-house legislature, and two court systems
The home is the foundation of civilization, and religion belongs to the home
Every pupil is raised to be a skilled, self-supporting artisan
Workers become shareholders, and competition moves toward service
Dignified insurance instead of charity, and a strictly kept public trust
Government without debt, light property taxes, five federal revenues
Schools of statesmanship train officials and judges
Voting by functional groups, with extra votes for service
Stern methods that the paper itself calls shocking
A strong defense that is never used for aggression
Urantia, with the Spirit of Truth, is better prepared
72.b55.box: Even one nation on an isolated world built an advanced government on the home, education, and service; Urantia, having received the Spirit of Truth, can prepare for a greater peace.
73.title: The Garden of Eden
73.b0.ask: “In a world darkened by rebellion, why did people tend a garden for a Son who had not yet come, and what became of that beautiful Garden?”
73.b2.p: In Paper 72 we looked at a nation on a neighboring planet that had suffered a rebellion much like ours. Paper 73 returns to Urantia and tells how the most beautiful place in our history, the Garden of Eden, was made ready. The Caligastia downfall had wrecked culture and spiritual life, yet it had little effect on the physical and biologic status of the races. Organic evolution went on apace.
73.b3.p: Almost forty thousand years ago the Life Carriers saw that the biologic development of the Urantia races was nearing its apex. Together with the Melchizedek receivers, they petitioned the Most Highs of Edentia to send a Material Son and Daughter. Tabamantia came to inspect the planet and recommended the request, and in a little less than one hundred years Adam and Eve arrived. They took up the difficult task of untangling the affairs of a planet retarded by rebellion and resting under spiritual isolation.
73.b4.p: Who, then, prepared a garden to receive them before they came, and in what faith? And what finally happened to that Garden and to the tree of life that grew within it?
73.b5.q: ⟦Q 73:3.6⟧Eden was the one bright spot on Urantia⟦/Q⟧
73.b8.p: On a normal planet the arrival of a Material Son heralds a great age of invention and intellectual enlightenment, but not so on Urantia. Ten thousand years after the rebellion nearly all the gains of the Prince’s administration had been wiped out, and the tribes languished in savagery. The traditions of Dalamatia and the culture of the Planetary Prince survived among only two groups.
73.b9.t: Descendants of the rebel members of the Prince’s staff, named after their first leader, Nod; they formed the eighth race of Urantia
Descendants of the Andonites who stayed loyal with Van and Amadon; more a cultural and religious name than a racial one
73.b10.p: A traditional enmity divided the two groups, and even later, in the affairs of Eden, it was exceedingly difficult for them to work together in peace. After the fall of Dalamatia the Nodites split into three groups: one near the head of the Persian Gulf, one in the highlands of Elam, and one on the Syrian shores of the Mediterranean. Some of them joined Van near Lake Van, mixed with the Amadonites, and were numbered among the “⟦Q 73:1.6|77:2.3|77:5.9⟧mighty men of old.⟦/Q⟧” Before Adam and Eve came, these two peoples were the most advanced and cultured races on earth.
73.b12.p: For almost a hundred years before Tabamantia’s inspection, Van and his associates had been preaching from their highland headquarters that a promised Son of God would come — a racial uplifter and a teacher of truth. Most of the world showed little interest, but those close to Van and Amadon took the teaching seriously.
73.b13.p: Van knew that the Material Sons on Jerusem always lived in simple but charming garden homes. So, eighty-three years before Adam and Eve arrived, he proposed that his people prepare such a home for them. More than three thousand volunteers from sixty-one settlements pledged themselves in solemn assembly to prepare for the promised — at least expected — Son. Caligastia and Daligastia did all they could to hinder the work, but almost ten thousand loyal midway creatures largely offset their schemes.
73.b14.t: Over three thousand, from sixty-one settlements
One hundred companies, each with a captain and a liaison officer
Sent out to find the ideal spot
Almost ten thousand loyal midway creatures
73.b16.p: After almost three years of searching, the committee on location reported on three possible sites and almost unanimously favored the third. It took two years to move the world’s cultural headquarters, including the tree of life, to the new place.
73.b17.t: 1. An island in the Persian Gulf
Later used for the second garden
3. A long, narrow peninsula on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean
Chosen — it was almost an island
73.b18.p: Ringed by mountains, the peninsula enjoyed a healthful climate and an even temperature. It seldom rained in Eden itself, but each night a “⟦Q 73:3.3⟧mist would go up⟦/Q⟧” from the irrigation channels to refresh the plants. Four tributaries rising in the peninsula’s coastal hills fed a great river; these were the “four heads” of the river which “⟦Q 73:3.4⟧went out of Eden.⟦/Q⟧” The surrounding mountains were rich in precious stones and metals, but the ruling idea was the glorification of horticulture and the exaltation of agriculture.
73.b19.q: ⟦Q 73:3.6⟧Without and beyond, the world lay in darkness, ignorance, and savagery. Eden was the one bright spot on Urantia⟦/Q⟧
73.b21.p: The dwelling place of the Material Sons is often called the Garden of Eden because it reflects the floral beauty of Edentia, the constellation capital. Van gave the entire peninsula over to the Garden. His instructions were plain: Eden was to be a garden, and only a garden. No animal was ever slaughtered within its bounds.
73.b22.t: A brick wall across the neck of the peninsula — the first task
The space between held wild beasts, a zoological garden and an extra line of defense
Walled paths led between the divisions to the Garden’s twelve gates
The river and its adjoining pastures
73.b23.p: Only volunteers built the Garden; no hirelings were ever used. The workers supported themselves by farming and herding, and believers nearby sent gifts of food. When Van suggested that the younger generation also be trained, in case the Son’s arrival was delayed, many took it as a lack of faith, and there were many desertions. Van went ahead with his plan of preparedness and filled the empty places with younger volunteers.
73.b25.p: At the center of the Edenic peninsula stood the stone temple of the Universal Father, and the other facilities were laid out around it. The plans provided homes and abundant land for one million people.
73.b26.t: The temple of the Universal Father, the sacred shrine of the Garden
Homes for the workers and their families
Ground for the schools of the expected Son’s educational system
Dwellings for the promised Son and his immediate offspring
73.b27.p: When Adam arrived, the Garden was only one-fourth finished, yet it already had thousands of miles of irrigation ditches, more than twelve thousand miles of paved paths and roads, and just over five thousand brick buildings. Its sanitation was far ahead of anything yet tried on Urantia: the drinking water was carefully protected, waste was buried, and later a covered brick-conduit disposal system was built. Many modern vegetables and cereals were first cultivated here. As the book says, never before or since has Urantia harbored such a beautiful and replete exhibition of horticulture and agriculture.
73.b29.p: In the center of the Garden temple Van planted the long-guarded tree of life. He knew that Adam and Eve, once they appeared in material form, would also depend on this gift of Edentia to sustain their lives. The “⟦Q 73:6.3⟧tree of the knowledge of good and evil⟦/Q⟧” may be a figure of speech, but the tree of life was no myth; it was real.
73.b30.t: A shrub of Edentia, sent when Caligastia was commissioned as Planetary Prince
Grew in the central, circular courtyard of the Father’s temple
Regrown from its core by Van; it sustained Van and Amadon for more than 150,000 years
Transplanted to the courtyard of another temple to the Father
Burned with the temple during one of the Nodites’ internal wars
73.b31.p: The fruit of this tree was like a superchemical storage battery, holding space-energies that counteracted the aging of animal existence. Yet it was wholly useless to ordinary evolutionary beings; it helped only those who had a complementary endowment. So when the Nodites were told they would become as “⟦Q 73:6.7⟧gods if they partook of the fruit of the tree,⟦/Q⟧” they ate of it for years and gained nothing, and they grew enraged. Now all flesh on Urantia takes the natural course of life and death, and Adam, Eve, and their descendants likewise came under the ascension plan in which mansion world resurrection follows material death.
73.b33.p: After Adam left the first garden, it was occupied by one group after another. Almost four thousand years later, amid volcanic activity and the sinking of the land bridge to Africa, the eastern floor of the Mediterranean sank and carried the whole peninsula beneath the waters. The sinking was gradual and took several hundred years. The book regards this as a natural occurrence, not a miscarriage of the divine plan or the result of Adam and Eve’s mistakes. Still, it notes that the sinking came at just about the time the reserves of the violet race were gathered to undertake the rehabilitation of the world.
73.b34.p: The Garden was never meant to be the permanent home of the Adamites. The Melchizedeks advised Adam not to begin the program of racial uplift until his own family numbered half a million. The Adamites were to become messengers of new life to all the world. Adam and Eve were to move among several world capitals as advisers and co-ordinators of a world-wide ministry of biologic uplift, intellectual advancement, and moral rehabilitation.
73.b35.q: ⟦Q 73:7.3⟧they were to mobilize for unselfish bestowal upon the needy races of earth.⟦/Q⟧
73.b37.p: Paper 73 is the story of people who, in a world darkened by rebellion, spent decades tending a garden in faith for a Son who had not yet come. Van and Amadon, more than three thousand volunteers, and the unseen midway creatures built an Eden that was the one bright spot on Urantia, with the Father’s temple and the tree of life at its heart. Yet the Garden was never a home to stay in; it was a starting point for going out. From there the Adamites were to gather their strength and give themselves to the whole world. In the end the Garden burned and sank beneath the sea, but its meaning — faith that prepares and love that gives itself unselfishly — lives on in the story handed down to us.
73.b38.t: The culture of Dalamatia survived only in two feuding groups
Van and the volunteers prepared in faith for a Son who had not yet come
Eden, on a Mediterranean peninsula, was the one bright spot in the world
Eden was to be a garden, and only a garden, and volunteers built it
An advanced city and farmland grew up around the Father’s temple
The tree of life was real, but it did nothing for ordinary mortals
The Garden sank, but it was always meant as a place to go out from
73.b40.box: Eden was the work of people who prepared in faith for a Son not yet come; it was never a home to stay in, but a starting point for giving themselves to the whole world.
74.title: Adam and Eve
74.b0.ask: “When Adam and Eve came to an isolated world, why did they refuse worship and point only to the Father?”
74.b2.p: In Paper 73 we saw how Van, Amadon, and their followers prepared the Garden of Eden to receive Adam and Eve. Paper 74 now brings us to the moment when the Material Son and Daughter at last arrive. Adam and Eve came to Urantia 37,848 years before A.D. 1934, in midseason, when the Garden was in the height of bloom.
74.b3.p: Their bodies were rematerialized over ten days within the precincts of the Father’s temple, and the two regained consciousness at the same moment. Material Sons and Daughters always serve together; it is the essence of their service never to be separated. This paper follows them through their first week, their administration, their home and schools, and even the roots of the creation legends that arose long afterward.
74.b4.p: What did these two beings teach first in a world cut off by rebellion? And what path did they choose when people wanted to bow down to them as gods?
74.b5.q: “⟦Q 74:4.5⟧Go you now to the material emblem of the Father’s invisible presence and bow down in worship of him who made us all and who keeps us living.⟦/Q⟧”
74.b8.p: The Adam and Eve of Urantia belonged to the senior corps of Material Sons on Jerusem and were jointly number 14,311. They were of the third physical series and stood a little more than eight feet tall. For more than fifteen thousand years they had directed the division of experimental energy as applied to the modification of living forms, and long before that they had taught in the citizenship schools for new arrivals. The book asks us to keep this background in mind as we read of their later conduct.
74.b9.p: When volunteers were called for, the entire senior corps offered themselves, and the Melchizedek examiners made the final choice. Although Adam and Eve had stayed loyal to Michael during the rebellion, they were still examined and instructed, and they were advised to regard themselves as subject to the Melchizedek receivers until that body chose to give up rule. They left behind a hundred children on Jerusem — fifty sons and fifty daughters — and departed amid the acclaim and good wishes of its citizens.
74.b10.t: Senior corps of Material Sons, jointly number 14,311
Third physical series, a little over eight feet tall
Directors of experimental energy for modifying living forms (over 15,000 years)
Teachers in the citizenship schools for new arrivals
Fifty sons and fifty daughters, all faithful stewards of universe trust
74.b12.p: Adam and Eve fell asleep on Jerusem and awoke in the Father’s temple on Urantia, face to face with Van and Amadon. The tongue of Eden was Amadon’s Andonic dialect, which Van and Amadon had improved with a new alphabet of twenty-four letters, and Adam and Eve had mastered it before leaving Jerusem. Carrier pigeons spread the news, and for months pilgrims poured into Eden.
74.b13.p: At noon a reception committee of twelve welcomed the pair. Then the chief of the Melchizedek receivers handed over the charge of the planet, and Van proclaimed them rulers of Urantia, giving up the titular authority he had held for over one hundred and fifty thousand years. The voice of Gabriel decreed the second judgment roll call. The dispensation of the Prince had passed, and the age of Adam, the third planetary epoch, had begun.
74.b14.t: One representative from each of the six races
Annan, a loyal daughter and spokesman
74.b15.h: 3. Adam and Eve Learn about the Planet
74.b16.p: Once installed, the pair became painfully aware of the planet’s isolation. The familiar broadcasts were silent, and the circuits of extraplanetary communication were gone. Their fellows had gone to worlds that were running smoothly, but here the deposed Prince was still present. That first night they walked and talked far into the night — and it was so lonely. On the second day they came to a full realization of the folly of trying to achieve planetary progress apart from the divine plan.
74.b17.p: On the sixth day Adam amazed his companions by naming animal after animal at a glance, describing its origin, nature, and function. He was one of the most expert anatomists in all Satania, and Eve was just as skilled. But this brilliance so overwhelmed the people that most of them were ready to fall down and worship the pair as gods.
74.b18.t: Installation; they felt the isolation and walked late into the night
Sessions with the receivers; they learned the results of the rebellion
An aerial tour of the Garden on the fandors
Addressed the Garden assembly; a council of men and women was chosen
Inspected men and animals; Adam named the animals
74.b19.p: The council chosen on the fourth day included women as well as men. This had not happened on earth since the days of Dalamatia, and seeing Eve share the honors and responsibilities of world affairs with a man was an astounding innovation.
74.b21.p: On the night after the sixth day, hundreds of well-meaning people who could not understand the simplicity of their new rulers decided to worship Adam and Eve as gods. Van protested but was brushed aside, and he sent the leader of the midwayers in haste to Adam. Early on the morning of the seventh day, Adam explained the orders of divine sonship and made it clear that only the Father and those whom he designates may be worshiped. Adam would accept any honor and all respect — but worship never.
74.b22.q: “⟦Q 74:4.5⟧And let this act be the sincere pledge that you never will again be tempted to worship anyone but God.⟦/Q⟧”
74.b23.p: The Material Son and Daughter stood alone on the mount with bowed heads, while the people bowed down around the temple. This was the origin of the Sabbath-day tradition. In Eden the seventh day was given to self-culture.
74.b26.p: For almost seven years the Melchizedek receivers stayed on duty and then returned to Jerusem; Van and Amadon were translated at the same time they left. Adam encouraged the arts of manufacture to build trade, and by the time Eden was disrupted there were over a hundred primitive manufacturing plants and wide trade relations with nearby tribes.
74.b27.p: But his effort to establish a world government met the direct and well-planned resistance of Caligastia and Daligastia as soon as it reached beyond the Garden. The fallen Prince had been deposed but not removed from the planet, and because he was invisible to mortal eyes, it was very hard to warn the races against him. Some confused minds, drawn to the teaching of unbridled personal liberty, kept upsetting Adam’s plans, so he withdrew his program for immediate socialization and fell back on Van’s method of organization. Instead of representative government he set up almost a hundred outlying centers, and the sending of ambassadors between tribes dates from his time.
74.b28.t: Socialization plan withdrawn because of resistance outside the Garden
About a hundred outlying centers ruled by strong individuals in Adam’s name
Group control by companies of a hundred and groups of ten
The practice of sending ambassadors between tribes began
74.b29.h: 6. Home Life of Adam and Eve
74.b30.p: The Adamic family grounds covered a little over five square miles, with provision for more than three hundred thousand descendants, but only the first unit of buildings was ever finished before the Eden plan collapsed. Adamson was the first-born. Before the default Eve bore sixty-three children, and when the pair left the Garden their family numbered 1,647 pure-line descendants over four generations.
74.b31.p: There was no cooking in Adam’s household; they ate fruits, nuts, and cereals once a day, and took in “⟦Q 74:6.4|3:2.4|41:3.1⟧light and energy⟦/Q⟧” from space emanations together with the tree of life. Their bodies gave off a shimmer of light, but since clothing hid most of it, only the glow from their heads could be seen — the origin of the tradition of the halo. They could exchange thoughts over about fifty miles, but this power stopped at once when the mind surrendered to the discord of evil. The play and humor of today’s races largely come from the Adamic stock.
74.b32.t: No cooking; fruits, nuts, and cereals, once a day
A glow around the head — the origin of the halo tradition
Thought exchange over about fifty miles
Own schools until sixteen, the younger taught by the elder
Betrothal at eighteen, two years of preparation, marriage at twenty
74.b34.p: Adam’s children were taught by the methods of the Jerusem schools until sixteen, and from sixteen to twenty they studied — and also taught — in the Urantia schools at the western end of the Garden. The whole purpose of the western schools was socialization; religious and sexual training belonged to the home and the parents. The Garden was open to visitors, but to live there a person had to be “adopted” and declare loyalty to the social rule of Adam and the spiritual sovereignty of the Universal Father.
74.b35.t: Health and the care of the body
The golden rule, the standard of social intercourse
Individual rights in relation to group rights and community obligations
History and culture of the various races
Ways to advance and improve world trade
Co-ordination of conflicting duties and emotions
Play, humor, and competitive substitutes for physical fighting
74.b36.t: The civil codes of the golden rule
The seven commands of supreme moral rule
74.b37.p: The moral law of Eden was much like the seven commandments of Dalamatia, but the Adamites taught more reasons for them. For instance, the indwelling of the Thought Adjuster was presented as an additional reason not to destroy human life. Adam discouraged set prayers, teaching that effective prayer must be wholly individual, the “⟦Q 74:7.21⟧desire of the soul,⟦/Q⟧” and he tried to replace blood sacrifices with offerings of the fruit of the land. He also taught sex equality: the woman, equally with the man, contributes the life factors that form a new being. Although the great plan of racial uplift was never carried out, the book says that tremendous gains still came from the small amount of Adamic blood the evolutionary peoples happened to receive.
74.b39.p: The story that the world was made in six days grew out of the tradition that Adam and Eve spent just six days on their first survey of the Garden, and the legend itself arose more than thirty thousand years later. The story of Eve made from Adam’s rib is a confused memory of the exchange of living substances when the Prince’s staff arrived, and the belief that man was made from clay spread across the Eastern Hemisphere. Away from the influence of Dalamatia and Eden, people more often believed in the gradual ascent of the human race.
74.b40.t: Adam and Eve’s first six-day survey of the Garden
The worship of the Father after the first upheaval
Confused with the exchange of life substances for the Prince’s staff
Sudden appearance of sun and moon
Possibly the world’s emergence from a dense space cloud
The tradition that bodies were created for Adam and Eve
74.b41.p: The Old Testament creation account was written long after Moses, and after the Babylonian captivity a modified Mesopotamian version gained favor. Later translated into Greek, it deeply influenced Western thought and led to the ideas of a golden age and the fall of man — discouraging outlooks built on retrogression rather than progress. But the book is plain: the golden age is a myth, while Eden was real. Adam and Eve carried on in the Garden for one hundred and seventeen years, until, through Eve’s impatience and Adam’s errors of judgment, they turned aside from the ordained way.
74.b42.q: ⟦Q 74:8.14⟧The “golden age” is a myth, but Eden was a fact, and the Garden civilization was actually overthrown.⟦/Q⟧
74.b44.p: Paper 74 presents Adam and Eve not as the first humans of a myth but as a Material Son and Daughter who came, with long experience and a clear mission, to a world isolated by rebellion. In their first week they learned about the planet amid loneliness and disappointment, and when people wanted to worship them as gods, they firmly refused and pointed only to the unseen Father. Their schools, laws, and home taught the golden rule, sex equality, and personal prayer, but their plans moved slowly against the resistance of the unseen former Prince. The later legend of a six-day creation is a changed memory of that first week. Eden was real, and its failure was real too.
74.b45.t: A seasoned and loyal pair volunteered and were chosen
Van handed over authority and the third planetary epoch began
Adam and Eve Learn about the Planet
They spent their first six days learning, lonely, in an isolated world
Adam refused worship and had the people worship only the Father
Facing the unseen Prince’s resistance, he scaled back his plans
Home Life of Adam and Eve
A home of glowing bodies, play, and humor left traditions behind
They taught the golden rule, personal prayer, and sex equality
The six-day creation is a memory of the first week; Eden was real
74.b47.box: Adam and Eve refused to be treated as gods and taught the people to worship the Father alone; Eden was not a legend but a fact.
75.title: The Default of Adam and Eve
75.b0.ask: “How did a shortcut begun with good intentions become the evil that brought down Eden?”
75.b2.p: In Paper 74 we watched Adam and Eve arrive on an isolated world, refuse worship, and build schools, laws, and a home. Paper 75 tells how their mission fell apart. After more than a hundred years of effort, Adam could see very little progress outside the Garden, and he often told Eve that the situation seemed to demand some relief not included in the original plans.
75.b3.p: The two were loyal, but they were cut off from their own kind and deeply distressed by the sorry plight of their world. The narrator of this paper is Solonia, the seraphic “⟦Q 75:4.2|75:8.8|73:7.5⟧voice in the Garden,⟦/Q⟧” who spoke to the pair on that fateful night.
75.b4.p: How, then, did a plan made by honest people for the good of the world become evil? And was its failure truly the fall of mankind?
75.b5.q: ⟦Q 75:8.6⟧Perfection is our eternal goal, not our origin.⟦/Q⟧
75.b8.p: On a rebellion-seared and isolated Urantia, Adam’s mission was a formidable undertaking. On a normal world the first work of a Material Son and Daughter is to co-ordinate and blend the races, but on Urantia the races had never been purged of their retarded and defective strains, so such a project seemed just about hopeless.
75.b9.t: A world ready for religious unity
They had to begin anew with the simplest forms of belief
Hundreds upon hundreds of local dialects
Only indirect contact, through the angels
The Melchizedeks left early, deepening their loneliness
75.b10.p: In their loneliness their courage weakened, and sometimes their faith almost faltered. The book says that they would have succeeded in time had they been more farseeing and patient. But both of them, especially Eve, were too impatient. They wanted to see immediate results — and the results they got proved most disastrous.
75.b12.p: Caligastia often visited the Garden and urged compromise and short cuts, but Adam and Eve stood firm. Neither he nor his associate had power to influence anyone against his will. He was still the titular Planetary Prince of Urantia and was not finally deposed until the times of Christ Michael on Urantia.
75.b13.p: The fallen Prince gave up on Adam and tried a wily flank attack on Eve, using the upper strata of the Nodites, descendants of his former staff. Before they left, the Melchizedeks had warned Eve never to stray from her mate’s side — to try no personal or secret methods. She kept this faithfully for more than a hundred years, but she saw no danger in her increasingly private visits with a Nodite leader named Serapatatia. It all developed so gradually that she was taken unawares.
75.b15.p: Serapatatia became the leader of the Syrian confederation of Nodite tribes and brought most of his people over to Adam’s cause. He became one of Adam’s ablest lieutenants. The book stresses again and again that he was entirely honest and sincere, and that he never knew he was being used as a tool of Caligastia.
75.b16.p: While waiting for the violet race to grow, he suggested to Eve that if the Nodites could have a leader born partly of the violet stock, it would bind them more closely to the Garden. The plan matured in secret for more than five years, until Eve agreed to meet Cano, the leader of a friendly Nodite colony, in the twilight of an autumn evening. Moved by flattery, enthusiasm, and persuasion, Eve agreed to add her own little scheme of world saving to the divine plan. Before she quite realized what was happening, the fatal step had been taken.
75.b17.t: Planned to entrap Eve through the upper-class Nodites
Proposed the shortcut in good faith, never knowing he was a tool
A Nodite leader who believed the plan was right
Impatient, she carried out the plan in secret
75.b19.p: When the celestial life of the planet was astir, Adam heard the whole story from Eve for the first time. That night the voice in the Garden told them that they had transgressed the Garden covenant, disobeyed the instructions of the Melchizedeks, and defaulted on their oaths of trust to the sovereign of the universe. Here the paper draws a clear line between good, sin, and evil.
75.b20.t: The carrying out of the divine plans
A deliberate transgression of the divine will
The misadaptation of plans and the maladjustment of techniques
75.b21.p: The archangel custodian had warned them again and again that on the day they mixed good and evil they would surely become as mortals and die. But Cano had assured Eve that people with good motives could do no evil. The book’s verdict is clear: though the plan was carried out with entire sincerity and the highest motives, it was evil, because it was the wrong way to reach a righteous end and it left the divine plan.
75.b22.q: ⟦Q 75:4.6⟧it constituted evil because it represented the wrong way to achieve righteous ends, because it departed from the right way, the divine plan.⟦/Q⟧
75.b23.p: The biblical question “⟦Q 75:4.8⟧Where are you?⟦/Q⟧” is the record of the counsel the narrator gave the pair that night. Later generations tended to credit anything extraordinary directly to the personal intervention of the Gods.
75.b25.p: Adam was heartbroken, yet he felt only pity and sympathy for Eve. The next day he sought out Laotta, a Nodite woman, and deliberately did the same thing. The book says he was not beguiled; he knew exactly what he was doing. He chose to share Eve’s fate because he could not bear the thought of a lonely vigil on Urantia without her.
75.b26.p: The enraged Garden dwellers swept down on the nearby Nodite settlement and destroyed it, and Cano perished with it. Overcome with remorse, Serapatatia drowned himself in the great river. Adam wandered alone for thirty days, while Eve and the children lived through terror and grief. When the Melchizedek receivers returned seventy days after the default, Adam knew for certain that they had failed. A long and bitter war between the Adamites and the Nodites followed.
75.b27.t: He deliberately followed Eve to share her fate
Wiped out by the enraged Garden dwellers; Cano died too
Took his own life in dismay and remorse
Adam’s thirty days of wandering; the children’s long sorrow
A long and bitter war between Adamites and Nodites
75.b28.h: 6. Adam and Eve Leave the Garden
75.b29.p: When the Nodites marched on the Garden, Adam asked the Melchizedeks for counsel, but they could not interfere with his personal plans and told him only to do as he thought best. Adam had no liking for war, so he left the first garden to the Nodites unopposed and went out from Eden with some twelve hundred loyal followers.
75.b30.p: On the third day the seraphic transports from Jerusem arrived. Children of twenty and older could choose to stay or to go to Edentia, and two thirds chose Edentia; all the younger children were taken there. Having come with such high hopes, the pair went out in disgrace and lost more than three fourths of their children before even finding a new home.
75.b32.p: Gabriel appeared and pronounced judgment: Adam and Eve were adjudged in default for violating the covenant of their trusteeship as rulers. Yet the judges on Salvington cleared them of all charges of contempt of the universe government; they were not held guilty of rebellion. Instead they were reduced to the status of mortals. They lost their immortal status for two reasons.
75.b33.t: 1. Intellectual association with the mind-gravity circuit of the Spirit
Broken by mental disjunction; immortal status was lost
2. A dual circulatory system drawing on the superenergy of the tree of life
Access to the tree was denied them
75.b34.p: Caligastia did trap Adam and Eve, but he did not lead them into open rebellion. What they did was truly evil, but they were never guilty of contempt for truth, and they never knowingly joined in rebellion against the rule of the Father and his Creator Son.
75.b36.p: Adam and Eve fell from the status of Material Sons to that of mortal man, but that was not the fall of man. The history of the human race is one of progressive evolution, and the Adamic bestowal left the world’s peoples much improved. Adam should not be regarded as the cause of a curse on the human race.
75.b37.t: There was no fall; the race was in fact uplifted
He failed, yet greatly advanced civilization
Perfection is our eternal goal, not our origin
75.b38.p: The lesson of this paper is for all of us. On the way to Paradise, nothing is gained by impatiently trying to get around the divine plan with short cuts or personal inventions. And the very fact that such mistakes can happen is evidence that personality is alive in the universe. A mechanistic universe would have no disagreement, but ours is personal and progressive.
75.b39.q: ⟦Q 75:8.7⟧What a glorious universe, in that it is personal and progressive, not merely mechanical or even passively perfect!⟦/Q⟧
75.b41.p: Paper 75 does not tell the fall of Eden as merely a tale of evil scheming. Two weary souls in isolation and loneliness, a Nodite leader who honestly wished to help the world, and an impatience to see results right away all came together into a wrong method for a good end. The price was heavy: war and death, separation from their children, and reduction to mortal status. Yet the book says plainly that this was not the fall of mankind. The race was in fact lifted up by Adam’s contribution, and the very possibility of such failure shows that we live in a universe of personality, not a machine. Perfection is not where we start, but the goal toward which we walk with patience.
75.b42.t: Impatience grew out of the hardships of an isolated world
The fallen Prince targeted Eve instead of Adam
A shortcut planned by honest people was carried out
Even with good motives, a wrong method is evil
War, death, and long sorrow followed
Adam and Eve Leave the Garden
They gave up the Garden without a fight and lost most of their children
They became mortals for default, not for rebellion
There was no fall; perfection is a goal, not an origin
75.b44.box: There are no short cuts in the divine plan, and even failure bears witness that we live in a personal and progressive universe.
76.title: The Second Garden
76.b0.ask: “How did a Material Son and Daughter who had failed rise again in the second garden and leave behind a story of triumph?”
76.b2.p: In Paper 75 we saw Adam and Eve reduced to mortal status for their default and forced to leave the first garden. Paper 76 follows their life afterward. They could not go west, for they had no boats; the northern Nodites were marching from the north; and the southern hills were full of hostile tribes. The only way open was east, so they journeyed toward the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
76.b3.p: Along the way Cain and Sansa were born. Laotta, Sansa’s mother, died in childbirth, and Eve took Sansa to her bosom and raised her with Cain. Sansa grew up to be a woman of great ability; she married Sargan, chief of the northern blue races, and helped advance the blue men of her time.
76.b4.p: What, then, did these two, bearing the weight of their default, build in the second garden? And how did their story end?
76.b5.q: ⟦Q 76:6.4⟧It is the people who make a civilization; civilization does not make the people.⟦/Q⟧
76.b8.p: It took Adam’s caravan almost a full year to reach the Euphrates, and finding it in flood, they camped nearly six weeks before crossing. Word that the king and high priest of Eden was coming had sent the local people fleeing to the eastern mountains, so Adam found all the land he wanted already empty. The site had been one of the three original choices for the Garden, and the two rivers, together with a defense wall fifty-six miles long, protected it.
76.b9.p: But in the new Eden they had to accept crude ways of living. The first garden had been partly prepared for them, but the second had to be made by the labor of their own hands and in the “⟦Q 76:1.4⟧sweat of their faces.⟦/Q⟧”
76.b10.t: Prepared in advance by Van and Amadon
Cleared and worked by their own hands
On the journey they ate herbs and vegetables for the first time
Life in a garden made ready
The harsh realities of mortal existence
76.b12.p: Abel was the first child of Adam and Eve born in the second garden. He became a herder, and Cain became a farmer. In the first Eden Adam had tried to discourage animal sacrifice, but in the busy and spiritually depressed days of the second Eden he left worship in the hands of Nodite priests, who soon drifted back to the old ways. Abel taunted Cain that his own animal offerings were preferred, and he never failed to remind Cain that Adam was not his father. When the brothers were eighteen and twenty, Cain turned on Abel in a rage and killed him.
76.b13.p: The book uses Abel’s story to show the value of environment and education. A bad environment can badly spoil an excellent inheritance, at least in the younger years, while a good social setting and proper education are what allow a good inheritance to flourish.
76.b14.q: ⟦Q 76:2.6⟧Good social environment and proper education are indispensable soil and atmosphere for getting the most out of a good inheritance.⟦/Q⟧
76.b15.p: Cain, seen as a living symbol of the default, was led by fear and some remorse to repent. He had always scorned his father’s religion, but now he went to his mother Eve for spiritual help, and when he honestly sought divine assistance, an Adjuster came to indwell him. He went to the land of Nod, became a great leader among his father’s people, and all his life he promoted peace between the Nodites and the Adamites.
76.b17.p: Adam and Eve deeply missed the old Garden and the children taken to Edentia, but they bore their diminished estate with grace and fortitude. Adam spent most of his time training his children and their associates, and because of this, his death made little difference in the conduct of his people’s affairs.
76.b18.t: Founded a secondary center of the violet race north of the second Eden
Civil administration; Jansad succeeded Adam as head of the tribes
Founded the new order of worship
Began foreign missionary service to the surrounding tribes
76.b19.p: The Sethite priesthood was a threefold undertaking embracing religion, health, and education; its members served as priests, physicians, and teachers. The book warns us not to confuse these noble teachers with the commercial priesthoods of later times; their methods of education have never since been surpassed. The Adamites produced the third alphabet and kept up writing, metalworking, pottery, and weaving, laying foundations for much of modern art and science.
76.b20.t: Priests who led the religious ceremonies
Teachers in the schools of the garden
76.b22.p: Adam and Eve were the founders of the violet race, the ninth human race on Urantia. Its people had blue eyes, fair complexions, and light hair — yellow, red, and brown. The parents lived by dual nutrition, on both food and light, but their offspring did not inherit this; they had a single circulation. They lived long, yet with each generation their life span drew nearer the human norm.
76.b23.t: Dual nutrition from food and light
A single, human type of circulation
The fruits of the trees, no meat
Dairy products after the first generation
Kept for over a hundred years after the default
Far greater than the evolutionary races
Weaker the less Adamic life they carry
76.b24.p: The children of Adam were usually Adjuster indwelt and were not easily gripped by fear. The book explains that so much fear and disease persist in today’s races because the plan for racial uplift failed early, and our ancestors received very little of Adam’s life plasm. In the second garden Adam chose to leave as much of his life plasm as possible to the world, and the 1,570 men and women born in this way became the early beginnings of the mighty Andite race.
76.b26.p: Not long after the second Eden was founded, Adam and Eve were told that their repentance was acceptable and that they would be eligible to join the sleeping survivors. Their transgression had been an error of judgment, not the sin of deliberate rebellion. Soon after becoming mortal, they became aware of a new presence within them — a Thought Adjuster — and this knowledge greatly heartened them for the rest of their lives.
76.b27.q: “⟦Q 76:5.3⟧you will be called from the embrace of mortal slumber when I come to Urantia if the subordinate Sons of my realm do not send for you before that time.⟦/Q⟧”
76.b28.p: This message from Michael was both a comfort and a mystery to them. So they always proclaimed that a Son of God would someday come, and Adam held the hope that this strife-torn world might yet become the envied planet of all Nebadon. Eve died first, of a weakened heart; Adam lived 530 years and died of old age. They were buried in the center of the temple, which began the practice of burying pious people beneath the floors of places of worship.
76.b29.p: With Adam’s default, the presence of physical representatives of the universe government, which had lasted more than four hundred and fifty thousand years, came to an end. Yet the book says that this very darkness became the background against which Michael chose this world to reveal the loving personality of the Father. Urantia was the most unfortunate of planets — and also the most fortunate.
76.b31.p: Adam and Eve went to their rest with strong faith that they would awake on the mansion worlds, and they did not sleep long. On the third day after Adam’s death, in the twenty-sixth special resurrection of the Urantia series, they were repersonalized on the mansion worlds together with 1,316 of their associates from the first garden.
76.b32.t: Citizenship won through the worlds of ascension
Among the four and twenty counselors of Urantia
76.b33.p: So ends the story of Adam and Eve — a story of trial, tragedy, and personal triumph. They made a mighty contribution to the civilizing and biologic progress of the human race, but as their inheritance was diluted and submerged, the advanced civilization they left could not survive. The book sums up the reason in a single sentence: it is the people who make a civilization.
76.b35.p: Paper 76 shows what life after failure can look like. Adam and Eve lost the Garden prepared for them, worked new land by the sweat of their brows, and endured the tragedy of losing their son Abel. Yet they bore it all with grace and fortitude, taught their children, and saw the Sethite priests serve religion, health, and education together. That an Adjuster came to indwell the repentant Cain, and also Adam and Eve once they became mortal, tells us that sincere repentance opens a new way. They closed their eyes holding Michael’s promise, awoke again, and returned as sons of man to help their own world. In this way the story of default becomes a story of personal triumph.
76.b36.t: The second garden had to be made with their own hands and sweat
Environment and education are the soil of inheritance, and repentance brings an Adjuster
The Sethite priests served religion, health, and education together
The traits of the ninth race were diluted over the generations
Their repentance was accepted, and the darkness became the stage for Michael’s coming
Resurrected as sons of man, they returned to help their world
76.b38.box: Sincere repentance opens a new way even for those who have failed, and in the end it is people who make a civilization.
77.title: The Midway Creatures
77.b0.ask: “How did the midwayers, who are neither men nor angels, come into being, and why do they remain as permanent citizens of this planet?”
77.b2.p: In Paper 76 we followed Adam and Eve to the end of their lives in the second garden and to their awakening beyond. All through that story there were unseen helpers — the ones who ran to bring news to Adam and who carried Adam and Eve to the temple. These were the midwayers, and Paper 77 now takes them up directly. Most inhabited worlds of Nebadon have beings who live on a level about midway between mortals and angels, and so they are called midway creatures.
77.b3.p: Urantia has two orders of midwayers: the primary or senior corps, who appeared in the days of Dalamatia, and the secondary or younger group, who date from the times of Adam. To explain where the secondary midwayers came from, the paper also tells of the Nodite race, the tower of Babel, and Adamson and Ratta.
77.b4.p: Where, then, did these unseen neighbors come from, and what are they doing beside us now?
77.b5.q: “⟦Q 77:9.3⟧What the United Midwayers undertake, the United Midwayers do.⟦/Q⟧”
77.b8.p: The primary midwayers came from a unique interassociation of the material and the spiritual on Urantia. The hundred members of Prince Caligastia’s corporeal staff were supermaterial beings on Jerusem, without power to reproduce, but on Urantia they became material beings able to have material offspring. From a supermaterial, nonsexual liaison of a man and a woman of the staff, the first-born of the primary midwayers appeared. The book frankly says it cannot satisfactorily explain how this happened.
77.b9.t: The first-born came from the supermaterial liaison of one staff couple
Each couple was permitted to do the same; fifty were born
After a year of observation the Prince allowed unlimited reproduction
One thousand for each couple — 50,000 in all
77.b10.p: They served as the intelligence corps of the Prince’s administration, ranging far and wide to study and help the world’s races. But the planetary rebellion ensnared a little over four fifths of them. The loyal ones served the Melchizedek receivers under the leadership of Van.
77.b12.p: Half of the ancestry of the secondary midwayers came from the descendants of the rebel staff, so the book pauses to trace the Nodite line. When the sixty rebels of the staff had children, those children proved far superior to both the Andonite and the Sangik peoples in body, mind, and spiritual capacity. This was because the Satania life circuits in the bodies of the staff had altered the Andonic germ plasm.
77.b13.t: Staff members who followed Nod into rebellion
Modified Andonites who joined the rebellion
Total — ancestors of the eighth race
77.b14.p: This is the origin of the almost universal folk tale of gods who came down to earth and fathered a race of heroes with the daughters of men. The Nodites gradually mixed with the evolutionary peoples and declined. Traditions such as the very long reigns in the Sumerian king lists, or a man living over nine hundred years, arose from the long lives of early Nodites and from confusing the twenty-eight-day month with the year.
77.b16.p: After Dalamatia sank, the Nodites founded Dilmun. As they multiplied and began to intermarry with neighboring tribes, their leaders wanted to preserve their racial unity, so they adopted the plan of Bablot, a descendant of Nod, to build a temple with a great tower. The place later became known as Babel. After four and a half years of work, a bitter dispute arose over the purpose of the tower.
77.b17.t: A memorial of Nodite history and racial superiority
A center of commerce and art honoring the Dilmun culture
A center for worship of the Father, to atone for their ancestors’ rebellion
77.b18.p: The religious group was promptly voted down, for most resented the teaching that their ancestors had rebelled. The other two factions then fought until they were nearly wiped out, while the religionists fled south. About twelve thousand years ago the Andites tried to build the tower again, but the structure fell of its own pretentious weight.
77.b20.p: The war over the tower scattered the Nodites, and their culture declined for more than a hundred and twenty thousand years. Even so, in Adam’s time they were still an able people; some of the Garden’s builders and some of the ablest minds on Adam’s staff were Nodites. They formed four centers.
77.b21.t: The racial memorialists; they contributed to the later Assyrian stock
The advocates of culture and commerce; they joined the Sangik tribes
Kept their purity, then blended with the Adamites to become the Sumerians
Followers of Van and Amadon; Mount Ararat was their sacred mountain
77.b22.p: This explains why the Sumerians appeared so suddenly in Mesopotamia with a full-grown culture. Dilmun, the paradise of men and God in the Sumerian clay tablets, is a blended memory of the Nodite cities and Dalamatia. The northern Vanites taught that their moral law of seven commandments had been given to Van by the Gods on Mount Ararat.
77.b24.p: The other half of the ancestry of the secondary midwayers came from Adamson, Adam’s eldest son. He had thirty-two children in the first garden, and he was deeply grieved when his mate and all their children chose Edentia. After helping to defend and build the second garden, he set out north to find the land of the Vanites he had heard of as a child. After a little over three years he met Ratta, who claimed to be the last pure-line descendant of the Prince’s staff, and married her.
77.b25.p: They had sixty-seven children, and every fourth child was of a unique order, often invisible. Adamson knew of the primary midwayers, so he mated a male and a female of these unusual children, and this was the origin of the secondary midwayers. The Adamsonites kept a high culture near the Kopet Dagh, south of the Caspian Sea, for almost seven thousand years, and some of their gains later became part of the potential that blossomed into European civilization.
77.b27.p: While the primary midwayers had an almost superhuman origin, the secondary order came from pure Adamic stock united with a humanized descendant of the staff. Among Adamson’s children were sixteen of these unique progenitors, and each couple could produce a secondary midwayer every seventy days — something that had never happened on earth before and has never happened since. The sixteen parents lived and died as mortals, but their offspring live on, free of the limits of mortal flesh.
77.b28.t: The times of Adam (grandchildren of Adamson)
Numerals (1-2-3 the first, and so on)
Letters (A-B-C the first, and so on)
77.b29.p: After Adamson died, most of the secondary midwayers became an unorganized, unattached influence and still caused much mischief in the days of Machiventa Melchizedek. While Christ Michael was on earth they all made their final decisions, and the loyal majority came under the leadership of the primary midwayers.
77.b31.p: Of the 50,000 primary midwayers, 40,119 joined the Caligastia secession. Of the 1,984 secondary midwayers, 873 failed to align themselves with Michael and were interned on the day of Pentecost. The leader of the apostate secondary midwayers was Beelzebub, and some older writers called these rebels evil spirits and demons.
77.b33.p: Before Michael came, these rebels could actually influence the minds of certain inferior mortals. But since the Spirit of Truth was poured out upon all flesh, no disloyal spirit can ever again invade even the weakest human mind. The whole group of rebel midwayers is now held prisoner.
77.b34.q: ⟦Q 77:7.8⟧Since the day of Pentecost there never again can be such a thing as demoniacal possession.⟦/Q⟧
77.b36.p: Shortly after Pentecost the two orders were joined into one, and today the 10,992 United Midwayers are governed alternately by the senior member of each order. They do not eat, sleep, or reproduce, yet they share many human traits; they enjoy our humor and our worship, and they enter into our work and play. They are neither men nor angels, but they understand and sympathize with human beings, and they are indispensable to the seraphim who serve as personal guardians.
77.b37.t: Patrol and observe the invisible spirit realm of the planet
Always used in contacts with mortal beings
Assistants to the various orders of seraphim
77.b38.p: Many of the more literal deeds credited to angels — such as Peter’s release from prison — were actually done by secondary midwayers. Their chief work today is to be the unseen associates of the men and women of the reserve corps of destiny, and their work helped make possible the revelations of which this book is a part. But they have nothing to do with so-called spiritualism or “mediumship.”
77.b40.p: The seraphim come and go, but the midwayers remain. They are natives of the planet as well as its ministers, and they provide the one continuing regime that connects the changing seraphic administrations. Any of them could leave the planet, but each has pledged not to leave until released, and they are anchored here until the ages of light and life. Only 1-2-3 the first was released after Pentecost; he now serves among the twenty-four counselors.
77.b41.p: Midwayers come into being fully developed, yet they never stop growing in wisdom and experience. The civilization of Urantia is the joint product of mortals and midwayers. Human generations forget, but the midwayers remember, and their memory holds the traditions of our world — even the story of Jesus’ life and teachings was given to us in this way. As our elder brethren, they will keep working with us until peace truly reigns on earth and good will fills the hearts of men.
77.b42.q: ⟦Q 77:9.9⟧The generations of men forget; the corps of midwayers remembers, and that memory is the treasure house of the traditions of your inhabited world.⟦/Q⟧
77.b44.p: Paper 77 introduces neighbors we cannot see: the midwayers. The primary midwayers were born of the supermaterial union of the Prince’s staff, and the secondary midwayers came from the unique children of Adamson and Ratta. Woven between these two stories are the rise and fall of the Nodites, the division at the tower of Babel, and the memories of Sumer and Dilmun. Many midwayers joined the rebellion, but since Pentecost all of them are held in custody, and since the Spirit of Truth was poured out, no disloyal spirit can enter a human mind. The United Midwayers who remain help the seraphim, work with the reserve corps of destiny, and keep the memories humans have forgotten. As permanent citizens of this planet and our elder brethren, they will not leave this world until the day of light and life.
77.b45.t: Fifty thousand were born of the supermaterial union of the Prince’s staff
104 people carrying modified germ plasm began the eighth race
A tower meant to glorify the race ended in division and civil war
The scattered Nodites became the roots of Sumer and other centers
The secondary midwayers came from their unique children
A corps of 1,984, nearer to man, came into being
Since Pentecost no disloyal spirit can enter a human mind
10,992 of them help the seraphim and the reserve corps of destiny
The midwayers stay and keep the memory of this world
77.b47.box: Standing between men and angels, the midwayers are permanent citizens who will not leave this world — our elder brethren who walk with us until the day of light and life.
